titulo.texto: Model and Mural of the Tlatelolco Market

frase_gancho.texto: Hundreds of figures on a market day, before the Spaniards arrived.

puente_narrativo.texto: In this market, quetzal feathers were sold, and they were worth more than gold. Now look for an enormous headdress made from them, whose story includes a journey to Europe and a debate that has lasted centuries.

guion_corto.texto: It is market day in Tlatelolco, and the plaza is full. What you see is a modern scale model with hundreds of clay figures: nobles, farmers, artisans, hunters, and long-distance merchants. There are stalls selling food, pottery, jewelry, tools, and live animals. Tlatelolco was the twin city of Tenochtitlan, and its market amazed the Spaniards. There were no coins like today’s: people bought with barter, and also with cacao beans, cotton cloaks, and feathers filled with gold dust. The model is a museum recreation of the Late Postclassic, based on what the chroniclers of the sixteenth century recounted.

guion_largo.texto:
Close your eyes for a moment and imagine the noise: voices offering their wares, the haggling, the rustle of reed mats, the murmur of thousands of people. That plaza really existed. It was in Tlatelolco, the twin city of Tenochtitlan, and it was one of the largest markets the Spaniards saw when they arrived.

What you have in front of you is not an ancient piece, but a modern recreation. It is made up of hundreds of hand-modeled figures, and it relies on what sixteenth-century witnesses recounted. Hernán Cortés described the plaza in his letters and spoke of tens of thousands of people. Bernal Díaz del Castillo, one of his soldiers, relates that some of his companions had been to Constantinople and to Rome, and that none of them had seen a plaza so large, so orderly, and so full of people. The friar Bernardino de Sahagún, moreover, gathered the voice of the Mexica themselves, who described to him the sellers of each product and how they announced their wares. In this way, the model does not rely only on foreign eyes.

And indeed, it was not disorder. The market was organized into sections, and each product had its place: cloth and cloaks, pottery, medicinal herbs, cacao, hides, jewelry, feathers, and live animals. According to Cortés, there was even a house where judges settled the disputes that arose between buyers and sellers. A large market needs rules, and this one had them.

Notice how people paid. There were no coins like today’s. People bartered, and they also used as money cacao beans, cotton cloaks, and small feather quills filled with gold dust. Imagine buying your food with cacao beans: the very same seed from which the drink of the nobles was prepared served to pay for tamales.

Among the stalls mingle the pochtecas, the long-distance merchants. They left Tlatelolco carrying their goods for weeks, crossed distant lands, and returned with luxury products: turquoise, gold, cacao, jaguar pelts, and quetzal feathers. It is thought that, at times, they also served as the eyes of the empire: they traveled, observed, and reported what there was in each place.

Tlatelolco had its own history. It was founded when a group of Mexica separated from Tenochtitlan, and for decades it had its own ruler. In 1473 it lost its independence to its sister city, but it kept the most valuable thing: its market, which remained the center of trade.

That same plaza was the stage of the end. On August 13, 1521, the last resistance of the Mexica against the Spaniards and their allies fell in Tlatelolco. A place of exchange and abundance was also the last place of a city that was defending itself.

Before going on, find a scene and give it a name. Who is buying? Who is selling? What is that woman holding in her hand? This museum is made of stone, but also of people who haggled, who greeted one another, and who went home with their baskets full.

texto.Period: Represents the Late Postclassic; modern scale model
texto.Origin: Recreation of the Tlatelolco market, twin city of México-Tenochtitlan

texto.pregunta: Myth: The Mexica paid for goods in the market with gold and silver coins.
texto.respuesta: Reality: They did not use coins. They bartered and used as money cacao beans, cotton cloaks, and feathers filled with gold dust.
